topic: Multi-intent task decomposition for LLM tool and skill routing
name: LLMCompiler — An LLM Compiler for Parallel Function Calling
description: LLMCompiler (arXiv:2312.04511; Kim, Moon, Tabrizi, Lee, Mahoney, Keutzer, Gholami; ICML 2024) parallelizes sub-tasks decomposed from a single compound prompt by borrowing classical-compiler principles. It comprises three components: (i) a Function Calling Planner that generates a DAG of tasks with inter-dependencies, (ii) a Task Fetching Unit that dispatches tasks as their dependencies resolve and substitutes placeholder variables ($1, $2, ...) with upstream outputs, and (iii) an Executor that runs ready tasks in parallel. A Joiner step (prominent in the LangGraph reuse) dynamically replans or finalizes based on graph history. Reported up to 3.7x latency speedup, up to 6.7x cost reduction, ~9% accuracy improvement over ReAct, and up to 1.35x latency over OpenAI parallel function calling. Code: github.com/SqueezeAILab/LLMCompiler.
decomposition_method: LLM-prompted (zero-shot/few-shot) planner. The Function Calling Planner uses LLM reasoning to decompose the compound prompt into a set of tasks with inter-dependencies, generating an execution plan as a DAG. The user provides only tool definitions plus optional in-context examples; the prompt to the planner is pre-defined-prompt + tool-definitions + optional in-context-examples. No fine-tuned splitter is required (though the paper notes a fine-tuned model could make variable substitution more robust). Works with both closed (GPT) and open-source (LLaMA) models.
decomposition_granularity: tool call. Each sub-task is a single function/tool invocation node in the DAG, with arguments that may contain placeholder variables ($1, $2) referencing the outputs of preceding tool-call tasks.
ordering_strategy: topological (DAG) with parallel fan-out of independent branches, plus dynamic mid-chain re-planning. The planner emits a DAG; independent tasks execute in parallel while dependent tasks wait for placeholder resolution. Tasks are streamed from the planner so execution can begin before the full plan is generated. When intermediate (a priori unknown) results require it, a new DAG is generated (replanning).
decomposition_validation: No dedicated solvability/completeness/non-redundancy validator (unlike AOP). The system trusts the planner's split, relying on tool definitions and in-context examples to keep planner errors low (the paper reports only 3 planner errors across the full evaluation). Correctness is enforced indirectly via the Joiner, which inspects the full graph history and decides to replan or finish — a feedback check on results rather than an a-priori validation of the decomposition itself. [uncertain]
hierarchy_depth: flat DAG of tool-call tasks (single-level graph of sub-tasks connected by dependency edges); no nested milestone/sub-agent hierarchy. ParallelQA function-reference graphs average depth ~4, but this is dependency depth within a flat task set, not a milestone+step hierarchy.
router_type: graph planner — the planner plans a full DAG of tool-call tasks upfront (with streaming) and the Task Fetching Unit dispatches them; not a per-sub-task classifier. Includes a replan path (Joiner -> planner) for cases needing new plans.
routing_model: prompted LLM (same family as main model; GPT-3.5/GPT-4 or open LLaMA) acting as the planner, guided by tool definitions and optional in-context examples. No separate fine-tuned classifier, embedding similarity, or RL router. Rule-based variable substitution is handled by the Task Fetching Unit, not a learned model.
handles_ambiguity: best-effort pick. Tool selection per task is made by the prompted planner from the provided tool set; there is no explicit ambiguity-resolution mechanism, abstention, or user-clarification step. Ambiguity or planner mistakes are caught downstream by the Joiner, which can trigger replanning, but the system does not ask the user or model uncertainty (no POMDP/clarification). [uncertain]
fallback_behavior: retry with re-decomposition. If intermediate results indicate the plan is inadequate (or a task fails / produces unexpected output), the Joiner passes graph history back to the planner to generate a new DAG (dynamic replanning). No explicit human-escalation or abort path is described; unmatched intents would simply lead to replanning or a final-answer attempt. [uncertain]
skill_pool_scale_and_retrieval: full-context — all tool definitions are placed in the planner prompt (user supplies tool definitions + in-context examples). The paper targets latency/cost of executing a known toolset rather than scaling to hundreds/thousands of tools; there is no embedding retrieval, two-stage coarse-to-fine filter, or skill-tree traversal for large tool pools. Large pools would inflate planner prompt size. [uncertain]
router_agent_asymmetry: Not applicable / not studied — a single planner LLM both sees tool definitions and produces the plan; there is no separate executing agent with reduced skill information. [uncertain]
execution_pattern: DAG (mixed) with parallel fan-out. Ready (dependency-satisfied) tasks are dispatched to the Executor and run in parallel; dependent tasks wait for placeholder substitution. Streaming dispatch overlaps planning with execution.
parallel_vs_concurrent: Concurrent (truly simultaneous) execution of independent tasks by the Executor, distinct from a single API turn's multiple tool calls. LLMCompiler eagerly executes DAG tasks as their dependencies resolve, achieving real overlap rather than only batching calls in one model turn; it reports up to 1.35x latency gain over OpenAI's single-turn parallel function calling.
dependency_detection: explicit DAG from planner. The planner annotates inter-task dependencies via placeholder variables ($1, $2 referenced inside later tasks' arguments); the Task Fetching Unit treats a task as ready only once all referenced placeholders are resolved, so independence is inferred from the absence of placeholder references.
result_aggregation: LLM joiner. After tool executions, observations are joined: the Joiner re-reads the full graph history (task results) and either produces the final answer or routes back to the planner for replanning. (In the original paper this final synthesis step; the LangGraph reuse formalizes it as an explicit Joiner node.)
mid_chain_feedback: hard — explicit dynamic replanning. The planner can generate a brand-new DAG based on intermediate, a-priori-unknown Executor results; the Joiner decides whether to finish or hand control back to the (re-)planning agent, an explicit re-planning node.
benchmark_name: HotpotQA (1,500 entity-comparison queries), Movie Recommendation / MovieRec (500 queries from BIG-bench), ParallelQA (custom, 113 queries, 5-8 calls, avg depth ~4), Game of 24, and WebShop (interactive, vs ReAct/LATS/LASER).
multi_intent_coverage: Yes — explicitly. Benchmarks are built around compound prompts decomposable into multiple sub-tasks: HotpotQA needs ~2 concurrent searches + summarization (parallel, independent); MovieRec ~8 concurrent searches (parallel); ParallelQA mixes parallel and dependent calls; WebShop is highly inter-dependent (sequential). Covers parallel, sequential, and mixed.
accuracy_metric: outcome-based exact/answer accuracy per benchmark (e.g., QA answer correctness; Game of 24 solve rate; WebShop success rate and average score). The emphasis is on accuracy together with latency speedup and cost reduction rather than per-step process supervision. Reports up to ~9% accuracy improvement over ReAct alongside up to 3.7x speedup and 6.7x cost reduction (e.g., HotpotQA 1.8x speedup / 3.37x cost; MovieRec 3.74x speedup / 6.73x cost).
clarification_capability: Not measured. LLMCompiler has no when-to-ask vs when-to-answer mechanism and the benchmarks do not test clarification; under-specification is handled (if at all) via replanning, not by querying the user. [uncertain]
process_vs_outcome_eval: Outcome-only. Final answer / success-rate correctness is scored; there is no intermediate process-supervision (per-step) reward in the evaluation. [uncertain]
eval_stability: Live-tool / live-API evaluation (real search and tool calls; experiments dated Nov 2023 and Sep-Oct 2023), with a custom ParallelQA set. No virtual/cached API server (unlike StableToolBench), so absolute numbers are subject to API/tool drift over time. [uncertain]
integration_pattern: Standalone framework (planner + Task Fetching Unit + Executor) wrapping a chosen LLM and a user-supplied toolset; widely reused as a LangGraph node graph (planner -> task-fetching/executor -> joiner with conditional replan edge). In-context / prompted decomposer rather than an inference-engine-layer component.
latency_overhead: Planning adds an upfront LLM call, but this is mitigated by streaming the DAG (the Executor starts before planning finishes), so the planner cost is overlapped with execution. Net effect is large latency reduction overall (up to 3.7x faster, 6.7x cheaper than ReAct) despite the added planning step; replanning runs add extra planner calls and grow state. Exact token overhead per plan not separately quantified. [uncertain]
online_adaptation: Static at deploy. No bandit/RL or log-driven fine-tuning of the planner; behavior is fixed by the prompt, tool definitions, and in-context examples (within-query replanning is runtime adaptation, not cross-query learning). [uncertain]
adoption: Open-source (github.com/SqueezeAILab/LLMCompiler, ICML 2024); influential reference architecture re-implemented in LangGraph (official tutorial) and multiple community packages (e.g., PyPI llmcompiler). Research + open-source, not a single commercial product.
